title: What Tailwind is doing on a Hanabi site
metaTitle: Tailwind as a small set of choices
excerpt: Utility classes keep spacing and type decisions in the code. The point is a small set of repeated choices, and a page another person can still read.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance. The open shore fits a piece about keeping a site's spacing and type to a small set.
caption: A short scale is easier to keep than a long menu. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why use Tailwind on a marketing site?
faqs.answer: So spacing, type, and color stay attached to a small theme instead of drifting into one-off CSS. Utilities are the vocabulary. The theme is the decision. A class list should repeat those decisions, not invent a new margin for every section.

faqs.question: How do you keep utility classes readable?
faqs.answer: Constrain the theme to the colors, sizes, and spacing you actually use. Avoid arbitrary values such as one-off pixel margins and hex codes. When the same long class list appears twice, make a component. The page component should read as a hero, a list, or a band, not as a generated stylesheet pasted into JSX.

faqs.question: Does Tailwind replace performance work?
faqs.answer: No. Production builds should drop unused utilities, images still need real dimensions, and the headline should be in the HTML the server sends. Google's Core Web Vitals targets, including an LCP within 2.5 seconds and a CLS under 0.1, still apply. Utilities style the page, and they do not create the content or excuse layout shift.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
Tailwind for marketing sites, on a Hanabi build, is how spacing and type decisions stay in the code. The point is a small set of repeated choices. It is not a page that cannot be read, and it is not a license to invent a new margin on every section.

Utilities are a vocabulary. A vocabulary works when it is short, shared, and visible. A long string of one-off values is the same mess as a long stylesheet, only harder to see while you are typing it.

## A small theme, then utilities

Start in the theme, not in the markup. Define the roles you already agreed on. Paper, ink, line, and accent become color tokens. The type scale becomes a handful of sizes, with the families and weights you actually use. Spacing becomes the steps you are willing to see on a page: a tight step inside a control, a step between paragraphs, a step between sections. Name them. A marketing page that needs seventeen different paddings does not need seventeen paddings. It needs a decision.

Tailwind's defaults are a starting menu, not the brand. Turn off the scales you will not use, or agree that only a few keys are allowed. If every number from the default spacing scale appears in the site, you do not have a scale. You have the menu. Constrain `tailwind.config` so the allowed values match the design. Then the class `mt-8` means something a reviewer can remember, because there are few siblings it could have been.

Arbitrary values, the square-bracket syntax, are the leak. `mt-[13px]` and `text-[#1a1a1a]` bypass the theme. They are useful for a one-time rescue and poisonous as a habit. A review rule that is easy to keep: no arbitrary value unless the pull request says why the theme cannot express it. Most of the time the theme should grow a token, or the design should use a token it already has.

The page should still read as a page. A section component with a few utilities is easier to follow than a section with forty utilities copied from a generator. If a pattern repeats, and on a marketing site the patterns do repeat, make it a component. The component can use utilities inside. The call site stays short: a hero, a list, a closing band. Readable code is part of the deliverable. You will hand this repository to the client.

## What the utilities are protecting

They protect the decisions from drift. A padding utility from the scale cannot slowly become 12 pixels in one file and 18 in another unless someone forces it. A text color utility tied to ink cannot become a near-black that is not quite ink. The constraint is the point. Without it, Tailwind is just a faster way to write inconsistent CSS.

They protect layout from surprises when you reuse them. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) treat cumulative layout shift as a core measure, and a good score stays under 0.1. One-off spacing, injected after load, or a webfont that changes line breaks because the fallback was never checked, will move the page. A known scale does not remove that risk by itself. It makes the layout predictable enough to test. Reserve space for images. Set width and height. Use the spacing steps you already have so a late-loading block does not invent a new height.

Largest Contentful Paint has a target of 2.5 seconds in that same guidance. A marketing page usually paints a headline or a photograph as its largest element. Utilities do not fetch that photograph. They also should not become a reason to ship a pile of unused CSS, or a blocker that waits on client JavaScript before the headline exists. Use the framework's production build so unused utilities are dropped. Keep the headline in the server-rendered HTML. The class names style it. They do not create it.

Interaction to Next Paint, under 200 milliseconds for a good score, is a reminder that a marketing page can still feel slow if every hover runs a heavy animation. Utilities make it easy to add transitions. The motion card still applies: two durations, transform and opacity, nothing that forces layout on every frame.

## A page another person can read

Class lists get a bad reputation when they are unsorted and endless. Sort them in a consistent order, by hand or with a formatter, so differences show up in review. Group layout, spacing, typography, color. A reader should be able to find the color without parsing a novel.

Extract a component when the same list appears twice. Do not extract a component for a single heading that is used once. The goal is a file you can skim, not a taxonomy. On a Hanabi site the stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, and the pages are mostly static. A section component that takes a heading, a paragraph, and an optional action is usually enough. Props for every visual variation will recreate the arbitrary-value problem in TypeScript.

Avoid `@apply` as a way to hide long lists if the result is a stylesheet of named classes nobody can find. A small component is easier to locate than a custom class buried in a global file. Use `@apply` sparingly, for a true primitive, such as a focus ring you want on many elements. The focus ring is one of the few things that should look identical everywhere. A utility or a single class both work if there is only one definition.

Comments are rarely needed if the component's name is honest. `Hero`, `WorkList`, `Close`. A file called `Section2` with a comment that says "the about area" is a sign the name is wrong. Rename it. The utilities inside can stay quiet.

## What not to do with a generator

Pasting a full page of utilities from a generator, or from a chat session, feels fast and reads like a stranger's site. The spacing will not match your scale. The colors will be hex values in brackets. The type will be a face you did not license. Treat generated markup as a sketch on paper. Rebuild it with your tokens, or do not use it.

Do not use Tailwind as a reason to skip the cascade you still want. A base style for body color, background, and the focus ring belongs in the base layer, so a new page is already on paper and ink before anyone adds a class. Utilities then change the exceptions. If the base is empty, every page must remember to set the background, and one page will forget.

Do not fight the system with a second system. A module stylesheet full of bespoke classes, plus Tailwind for "the small stuff," means nobody knows where a value lives. Pick the utilities and the theme. A single CSS file for a third-party embed that you do not control is fine. A parallel design system is not.

Plugins deserve the same skepticism as arbitrary values. A plugin that adds a gradient palette you do not need will be used because it is there. Install little. Prefer a token you wrote, which you can name and delete.

## Review like a design review

Look at the pull request for new values, not only for new sections.

- Colors come from paper, ink, line, and accent.
- Spacing and type come from the named scale.
- Arbitrary values are either absent or explained.
- Repeated blocks are components, and one-off blocks are short.
- Images have dimensions so they do not shift the text.
- The headline is in the HTML the server sends.

Open the page with the stylesheet blocked in part, or with a forced reduced-motion setting, and confirm the words are still in order. Utilities are presentation. The document is the page. If the document only makes sense with a specific class string, you have hidden the structure. Put headings in headings. Put buttons in buttons. Then style them.

When the theme changes, change the token, not the call sites. That is the payoff you were protecting. An accent that moves from one blue to another should be a one-line edit. If it is a hunt through bracket values, the theme was never in charge.

Leave a short note in the theme file that a future editor can trust. List the color roles and the type sizes in plain language, above the tokens. When someone wants a tighter hero, they should see that section spacing is already a named step, and change the design to that step or change the token for everyone. A one-off on the homepage becomes the unofficial scale the moment a second page copies it. Read the class list out loud once during review. If you cannot say what the section is doing without decoding five arbitrary values, the markup is not ready to hand over.

## After the site is in the repo

The theme file is part of what the client owns. Leave it readable. A short comment at the top can list the roles and the type sizes in plain language, so a future edit starts from the decision and not from a guess. Keep the comment shorter than the config. The config is the decision.

Server rendering is the other half of a fast company site, and it is the next piece to read. [Server rendering for a company site](/blog/server-rendering-for-a-company-site) explains why the first view should arrive as HTML, with these classes already doing their work, instead of waiting on the browser to assemble the company.

When you want that constrained theme built into a site you can keep editing, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The utilities are there to repeat a few choices, on purpose.
